title: Polynomial Ring
body:
$F[x]$: all polynomials in one variable with coefficients from a [[Field]] $F$, added and
multiplied the usual way. It is a commutative [[Ring]] with 1, and an integral domain, but not a
field: $x$ has no inverse, since nothing multiplied by $x$ gives 1.

The point of the block is that **$F[x]$ behaves almost exactly like $\mathbb{Z}$**, and every
theorem from the number theory block reappears with degree in place of magnitude.

| $\mathbb{Z}$ | $F[x]$ |
|---|---|
| size $\lvert n \rvert$ | $\deg f$ |
| units $\pm 1$ | the non-zero constants |
| [[Division Algorithm]] | division with remainder, $\deg r < \deg g$ |
| [[Euclidean Algorithm]] | the same algorithm on polynomials |
| [[Prime Number]] | irreducible polynomial; see [[Irreducibility]] |
| unique factorisation into primes | unique factorisation into irreducibles |
| $\mathbb{Z}_n$ | $F[x]/(f)$, and it is a field when $f$ is irreducible |

That last row is the whole payoff and is what [[Field Extension]] and [[Finite Field]] are built
from.

## Degree

$\deg(fg) = \deg f + \deg g$ over a field, which is the fact that makes everything else work.
It needs no zero divisors: leading coefficients multiply to something non-zero because $F$ is a
field. Over $\mathbb{Z}_6$ it fails, since $2x \cdot 3x = 0$.

By convention $\deg 0$ is undefined or $-\infty$, so the formula never has to be qualified.

## Division with remainder

For $f, g \in F[x]$ with $g \ne 0$ there are unique $q, r$ with

$$f = qg + r, \qquad r = 0 \text{ or } \deg r < \deg g$$

This is long division, and it is where the field matters: you divide by the leading coefficient
of $g$ at every step, which needs an inverse.

```
divide x³ + 2x + 1 by x + 1, over Q

    x³ + 0x² + 2x + 1  =  (x + 1)(x² - x + 3) - 2
    q = x² - x + 3,  r = -2,  and deg r = 0 < 1 = deg g
```

Two immediate corollaries, both one line from the above:

- **Remainder theorem**: dividing $f$ by $x - a$ leaves the constant remainder $f(a)$.
- **Factor theorem**: $(x-a) \mid f$ exactly when $f(a) = 0$. Roots and linear factors are the
  same information.

So a polynomial of degree $n$ over a field has **at most $n$ roots**: each root peels off a
linear factor and drops the degree by one. Over a non-domain that fails, and $x^2 - 1$ has four
roots in $\mathbb{Z}_8$.

## Quotients

$F[x]/(f)$ is polynomial arithmetic mod $f$: reduce everything to degree $< \deg f$, exactly as
$\mathbb{Z}_n$ reduces everything below $n$. The elements are the possible remainders, so the
quotient has $\lvert F \rvert^{\deg f}$ elements when $F$ is finite. If $f$ is irreducible the
quotient is a field, by the same Bézout argument that makes $\mathbb{Z}_p$ a field: run the
[[Euclidean Algorithm]] on $g$ and $f$, get $ag + bf = 1$, and $a$ is $g$'s inverse.

Two things in the vault are this construction:

- $\mathbb{R}[x]/(x^2+1) \cong \mathbb{C}$. See [[Field Extension]] and [[Complex Numbers]].
- $\mathbb{Z}_2[x]/(x^8 + x^4 + x^3 + x + 1) = GF(2^8)$, the field a byte lives in. See
  [[Finite Field]].
